Ben_Bulben.json.text: Ben Bulben is an Irish mythological site. The peak rises on the coast above the town of Sligo. A mound of stone sits near its summit. The hero Diarmait Ua Duibne died beside it. A magical boar had carried the hero on its back. Diarmait killed the beast. He then brushed against its body and pierced himself on a poisonous bristle. Fionn Mac Cumhaill was a healer and could have saved him. He chose to taunt the dying man instead. Grainne, Fionn's intended wife, had loved the younger Diarmait for years. That love drained Fionn as he chased the pair across Ireland. The peak now shadows the grave of William Butler Yeats.

Bendonner.json.text: Bendonner is an Irish folk figure. This Scottish giant terrorized the coast of Ulster. The residents asked the giant Finn MacCOOL for help. Finn Mac Cool is a folk form of the hero Fionn Mac Cumhaill. Finn challenged Bendonner, then dressed in swaddling clothes. He posed as an enormous baby in an immense cradle. Bendonner saw the baby, feared its strength, and fled. He never troubled the coastal people again.

Benn_Étair.json.text: Benn Étair is an Irish mythological hill. It is now the Hill of Howth near Dublin. The site appears in many legends. In the tale of the Sons of Tuireann, the weary heroes said their strength would return once they saw Benn Étair. The hill may have held healing power. Aidin, the widow of the hero Oscar, was buried there by the bard Oisin. A fairy woman, Etain of the Fair Hair, lived on the hill. She died of grief when her mortal husband was killed. The hill is named for her father, Étair.

Berba.json.text: Berba is an Irish goddess. She is the tutelary goddess of the River Barrow. In the Book of Invasions, the goddess Cesair is also called Berba. Cesair was Ireland's first settler. Berba is the proper title of the Barrow's guardian. She keeps a place among the Irish river goddesses.

Berecynthia.json.text: Berecynthia is a Continental Celtic goddess. The early Christian writer Gregory of Tours gave the record of her. Her image, veiled in white, was carried through the fields each spring. The rite also ran when crops threatened to fail. She may be a form of the goddess Brigindo. Both act as regional fertility spirits. Martin of Tours destroyed most of the region's pagan idols. Because of this no image of Berecynthia is likely to survive.

Berrey_Dhone.json.text: Berrey Dhone is a Manx goddess. Her name means Brown Berry. She was a hag or witch on the Isle of Man. She lived on top of North Barrule Mountain or inside it. Like other forms of the Cailleach, she was a giant. Her rocky heelprint can still be seen on the mountainside.

Biddy.json.text: Biddy is an Irish name for the goddess Brigit. People used it on the spring feast of Imbolc. Children then went begging from house to house. In Kerry, white-garbed young men were the Biddy Boys. They sang a short verse for the poor. The custom faded late in the twentieth century. It has since been revived in Kerry itself.

Biddy_Early.json.text: Biddy Early was an Irish folk heroine. People called her the White Witch of Clare. She was a healer in the eastern part of County Clare in the 19th century. Her name still stands a century and a half later. She was a real woman of the parish of Feakle in the Slieve Aughty hills. The fairies were said to have given her a magical blue bottle. She looked into it to learn the cause of an illness. She often clashed with the local clergy. When she died she threw the bottle into a stream. Locals say it still rests there today.
